title: The hare in the moon
hook: a hare with nothing to give offers himself to a hungry guest; his image is set on the moon (Jataka 316)

segments.voice: Yesterday: parinibbana, and the last words: all things put together come apart, so keep going. Your line: strive on with care. A new week starts today: the Jataka, as shorts.

Tonight, if the sky is clear, look up at the moon. Some people see a face there. In stories told from India to Japan, people see a hare. Now the path turns to something lighter and very old: the Jataka tales, a great collection of stories that tradition says the Buddha told about his own earlier lives, as an animal, a king, a merchant, a monkey. They were painted on temple walls and carved on stone gates, and they're still told to children. The first one this week begins in a forest, with four friends: an otter, a jackal, a monkey, and a hare.
screen: `A HARE IN THE MOON.` → `THE JATAKA: EARLIER LIVES.` → `FOUR FRIENDS IN A FOREST.`

segments.voice: The hare is wise, and he teaches the others. One day he says: tomorrow is a holy day. Let's keep it well, and if anyone comes asking for food, let's give from what we have. Next morning, each goes out. The otter finds fish on a riverbank. The jackal finds some meat and a pot of curds. The monkey brings mangoes. But the hare only eats grass. I can't offer anyone grass, he thinks. If a hungry guest comes, I'll give him my own body. Sakka, the king of the gods, hears of this and decides to test it. Disguised as a hungry traveler, he visits each friend in turn. The otter offers fish, the jackal meat, the monkey mangoes. Then he comes to the hare, who says: gather some wood and make a fire. I'll give you something I've never given before. The fire is lit. The hare shakes himself three times, so any tiny creatures in his fur can escape unharmed. And he leaps into the flames. But the fire is cold. Not a hair on him is singed. The traveler reveals himself as Sakka, come only to test him. So that the hare's gift will be remembered, he draws the hare's image on the face of the moon, to last through this whole age of the world. Whatever anyone sees in the moon, the story's shape is plain. The hare had the least of anyone, and gave the most, the one thing he had. And even then, he shook himself first.
screen: `FOUR FRIENDS, ONE HOLY DAY.` · `THE HARE ONLY HAS GRASS.` · `HE SHAKES HIMSELF THREE TIMES.` · `DRAWN ON THE MOON.` · then, large: `GIVE WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Some days there doesn't seem to be much to give, not much money, not much energy. Ask yourself, like the hare: what do I actually have? Time, attention, a skill, a listening ear, a good laugh. Pick one, and picture giving it, fully, to someone who needs it.
Sasa. The hare who, with only grass to give, offered his whole self to a hungry guest, and whose image was drawn on the moon.
Your line: give what you have. Grass was all he had, so he offered himself. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jataka tales like the hare's are told to children, painted on temple walls and performed as plays across Buddhist Asia, and Buddhists hear in them the perfections, such as generosity, that the Buddha is said to have practiced over many lives.

fork.setup: you're the hare. a hungry traveler has come, and all you eat is grass. what do you offer?
fork.reveal: he asks for a fire and leaps in. it's cold: the traveler was Sakka, testing him, who draws the hare on the moon.

original.note: Pali: hare. The story is the Sasa Jataka, and the Sanskrit word for the moon, śaśin, means 'marked with a hare'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute folk tale about the moon.
what it means: a story of total generosity from the one with the least, told as one of the Buddha's earlier lives.
what a scholar hears: Sasa Jataka, no. 316; retold in Arya Shura's Jatakamala; Sanskrit śaśin, 'hare-marked', is a name for the moon.

sources.ref: Jatakamala of Arya Shura, the hare

notes: Jataka 316 retold in paraphrase; the Cambridge translation (Cowell ed., 1895–1907) is public domain but is not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.
Details to confirm: the jackal's find (meat, a lizard and a pot of curds in some versions); Sakka squeezing a mountain to draw the hare; the three shakes.
'Hundreds' of Jataka: the Pali collection has 547. Painted and carved (e.g. Bharhut, Sanchi, Ajanta): confirm phrasing 'more than two thousand years'.
Sanskrit śaśin/śaśāṅka as a name for the moon: confirm the note.
'You don't have to believe the moon has a hare on it' is meant lightly; confirm it doesn't read as dismissive.
